# @visio/styling design

Build-time styling for Solid 2. Typed style objects in, one atomic stylesheet out, tokens readable from JS, rendering-performance rules enforced by the compiler.

## Goals

1. Agent-safe: mistakes fail at build time with a message that names the fix.
2. One stylesheet, minified, grouped by condition, no CSS modules, no unused variables.
3. Token values and variable names available in JS without DOM reads.
4. The darkroom fluid system: design px scaled to the viewport, grid columns, per-screen overrides.
5. Solid 2 native: class arrays for composition, the `style` prop for runtime values.
6. Style hygiene at the project level: near-duplicate values, raw values that are tokens, unused tokens, overlapping class arrays.

## Pipeline

```
tokens.ts ──defineTokens()──► Tokens ──tokensToCss(used)──► tokens layer (+ @property), pruned
                                 │
component.tsx ──parse (oxc)──► scan ──► evaluate ──► normalize ──► atomize ──► registry
                                 │        │                                        │
                                 │        └── token refs, class arrays             └── emit() → Lightning CSS
                                 └── rewrite css() → { key: "atoms" }
```

- **extract** (`compiler/extract.ts`): scans imports, top-level consts, every call, every token member expression, and every `class` attribute (arrays for the overlap check, string literals for the hand-typed atom check). Rewrites `css()`, `css.recipe()`, `css.global()`, `css.keyframes()`, and `sizes()` with magic-string. Emits the overlap warning when two entries of a class array set the same property identity. Appends the static `sizes` of an element to the `?responsive` import it renders, so `@visio/image-optimizer` encodes only the widths that attribute can pick (see its DESIGN.md), and warns (`RESPONSIVE_NEEDS_SIZES`) at an import that reaches no such element and carries no `sizes` of its own.
- **evaluate** (`compiler/evaluate.ts`): restricted static evaluator. Literals, templates, arithmetic, object spreads, same-file `const`s, token members, the fluid helpers. Fluid helpers return a `FluidValue` that carries the design number, so nothing downstream has to parse a calc string. Records the source span of every object key by dotted path, which is what the source map is built from.
- **normalize** (`compiler/normalize.ts`): key classification, camelCase to kebab, shorthand expansion, unit checks, the type preset rule, single-declaration performance rules. Selector keys become templates with `&` for the element (`compiler/selector.ts`); nested templates compose by substitution. An `&` in a quoted string or after a backslash is text. `ampersands()` in `compiler/selector.ts` finds each `&` for the element, and each search or replacement of `&` uses it.
- **atomize** (`compiler/atomize.ts`): one class per `(conditions, selector, property, value)`, readable names, file ownership for HMR.
- **emit** (`compiler/emit.ts`): layers `tokens, reset, base, atoms`; atoms grouped per condition combination into one at-rule block, ordered so later conditions win and a combination comes after each condition it contains (`desktop: { hover }` beats `hover`). Every selector part except the atom class is wrapped in `:where()`, so all atoms have exactly one class of specificity and order is the only tiebreaker. A pseudo-element cannot sit inside `:where()`, so it stays outside. Container queries are just conditions whose prelude starts with `@container`. Each emitted line remembers the declaration that produced it.
- **project** (`project.ts`): the shared model. Loads tokens, compiles files, computes which variables are referenced anywhere (styles or JS), builds the pruned stylesheet with a source map from every rule back to the `.tsx` property, checks hand-typed atom names against the registry, and builds the report. The Vite plugin and the CLI are thin wrappers over it.
- **report** (`lint/report.ts`, `lint/values.ts`): project-wide findings. Raw values are parsed by Lightning CSS into typed lengths and colours; a value with `var()` comes back empty, and fluid values use the number carried by `FluidValue`. Every compiler warning is a finding too, with its style path or its line, so one rule decides what fails: every finding fails the build and `visio-styling check`. No option turns that off.
- **plugin** (`plugin.ts`, behind `vite.ts`): in a build, the first file with errors stops the scan, and the report prints at the end. In dev every message goes to the terminal, where an agent reads it. The scan at start logs every file's errors and keeps serving; `transform` still throws them when the file is requested. A save logs the file's errors once, when they change, before it throws them for the overlay: Vite sends an error from `hotUpdate` to the browser only. The report is built 200ms after the last scan, save, or sheet load, and its findings print when the list changes, with what they do to the build.

## Types first

A rule that needs only the literal goes in the types too, so the editor shows it while the agent types. `CSSProperties` has no key for a rejected shorthand (`border`, `transition`, ...): each is typed `Rejected<'Use borderWidth, ...'>`, a type no value fits, so the error names the longhands. A bare number fits only the unitless properties; any other property takes `0` or a string (`UnitValue`). `scrollBehavior` has no `smooth`. Both types read the compiler's tables (`REJECTED` and `UNITLESS_PROPS` in `compiler/props.ts`, camel-cased by a template type), so the two cannot drift. `css()` infers only the keys (`Record<K, Style>`), so every style is checked as a `Style` with excess property checks: a condition missing from `Conditions` or a misspelt property is a type error. A recipe's variant options are inferred whole, to keep their names for the props, so an unknown key in an option is left to the compiler; wrong values there still fail. A `FontSource` is a union: `axes` needs `subset`, a subset list has at least one entry, and `used` is not a list entry.

The compiler keeps every check. `unsafe` is typed as any property with any value, and a value the evaluator computes has no literal type, so the build is still the last word. `test/types.test.ts` holds the `@ts-expect-error` cases.

## The fluid system needs no compiler

`--frame` is `100vw`, or `min(100vw, layout.maxWidth)` when the tokens cap it. `--dp` is registered with `@property` as a `<length>` and set to `calc(var(--frame) / designWidth)` per screen: mobile at the root, then one `@media (width >= from)` block per other screen in ascending order (`screenStops()`), each at its `from`. A per-screen value (`Responsive<T>`) names `mobile` and `desktop` and may name `tablet` and `widescreen`; a screen without one takes the nearest smaller screen's (`resolveResponsive()`), so a tablet design is one more entry in `screens` and nothing else has to change. Each screen past mobile is a condition by its own name, ordered by width, so a tablet's atoms sit between mobile's and desktop's in the sheet. Browsers compute registered properties to pixels at declaration time, so `calc(24 * var(--dp))` is always exact and `getComputedStyle` returns resolved pixels. `--col`, `--gap`, `--safe` and `--columns` (the column count, an `<integer>`) follow the same pattern, all derived from `--frame`, so past the cap a full row of columns is `maxWidth` wide and a container with `max-width: var(--frame); margin-inline: auto` centres it. The JS `px()` readers use `viewport.frame` for the same reason. The viewport store they read installs on its first read, so importing the tokens module is safe during SSR. `dp()` and `columns()` are string templates that any tool could emit. `sizes()` is compiled to its string like `css()`, because a runtime registry filled by `defineTokens()` would be empty once the bundler drops a tokens import used only in compiled calls. Its `height` option resolves `dp()` and `dph()` the way `--dp` and `--dph` do on each screen, because a `sizes` attribute cannot read a custom property, and writes `width / height` for `<Image>` to finish with the image's ratio (`@visio/image-optimizer` DESIGN.md).

## Accessibility of scaling

A design px is worth less than a CSS px on every viewport narrower than its design, so text and pointer targets shrink with the window; the desktop breakpoint is the worst case because the desktop design is shown at `desktop.from / desktop.width` there. Text has a floor, so the report does not check it. `lint/a11y.ts` measures blocks with `cursor: pointer` for `TARGET_TOO_SMALL` against 24px, the WCAG 2.5.8 minimum, where each design renders smallest: mobile at a 320px viewport, every other screen at its start. It reads an explicit scaled height or width, otherwise an estimate from the paddings plus one line of the block's font size and unitless line height. Recipe variants are composed over the base and only reported when they change the box; a fixed size on an axis ends the check for it. The compiler also records how every styled JSX element composes its blocks (`class={[s.a, cond && s.b]}` is two compositions, `a` and `a + b`, a later block winning per property) and which styled DOM element is its nearest parent, looking through Solid control flow but not through components or unstyled elements. Compositions are measured as one box, once each; a block no element composes is measured on its own. A child without a height of its own takes it from a parent that is a grid with a single scaled `grid-auto-rows`, or a flex row with a scaled height, minus the parent's padding, unless either side opts out of stretching. A block that spreads `HIT_AREA` (`src/presets.ts`) passes on each axis whose two `::before` insets are `HIT_AREA_INSET`: the pseudo-element reaches 44px each way whatever the box measures, so the target grows and the layout does not. It counts per screen, as each inset in effect there; an `overflow-x` or `overflow-y` other than `visible` on the element clips the pseudo-element, so it does not count; and a later block in a class array replaces a `::before` inset only with a `::before` inset, never with the element's own. The compiler reads `SR_ONLY`, `HIT_AREA` and `GRID` as it reads a token preset; they are the only style objects a site imports from the package. `GRID` is `repeat(var(--columns), minmax(0, 1fr))` with `var(--gap)` between: on the content width its tracks are `--col` wide, and `minmax(0, …)` keeps a long word from widening one.

The floor is always on: `normalize` wraps every scaled `font-size` in `max(calc(n * var(--dp)), 0.75rem)`, so text never renders under 12px. The pointer-target estimate uses the floored size. The 320px viewport, the 12px floor and the 24px target are fixed (`A11Y` in `tokens/index.ts`); the tokens have no `a11y` key, because a site that turns the floor off or lowers a threshold only hides a problem. Unitless line heights and em tracking follow the font size, so a preset keeps its shape at the floor. The `rem` also gives the browser's text size setting a way in.

Browser zoom is the one thing scaling ignores: zoom halves the CSS viewport, `--dp` halves with it, and the page renders the same physical size (WCAG 1.4.4). The floor helps once text has hit it; a cap helps once the window is wider than twice `maxWidth`. Neither makes viewport-scaled type respond to zoom in general.

Mixing a rem share into `--dp` was built and measured (2026-09-09) and rejected. Anchored so the design stays exact at its own widths, a half-rem unit grew the heading about 15% at 150% zoom while halving fluid scaling everywhere: with the 1260 cap the desktop range swing went from 57% to 22%, and the site read as not scaling at all. A smaller share gives back scaling and gives up the zoom gain in the same proportion, since they are one number. What zoom does today, measured on a 1440 window: body text grows through the floor (14, 16, 18 physical px at 100, 125, 150%), headings do nothing until the breakpoint flips at 180%, then everything jumps to the mobile design stretched across the zoomed viewport. Zoom detection in JS is not reliable across browsers. The remaining lever is a floor on the unit itself, which changes narrow desktop windows the same way and is a design decision, not an accessibility patch.

### Fluid off

`fluid: false` in the tokens sets `--dp` and `--dph` to `calc(1rem / 16)` once, at the root, for a client that forbids viewport scaling. It is rem, not `1px`, because the usual reason to forbid scaling is that viewport-sized text ignores the browser's text size setting, and `1px` would ignore it too. Nothing else changes: `dp()` and the compiler are the same, per-screen values still switch at each `from`, and `--col` still divides the frame, so the grid fills the window with fixed gaps and margins. `sizes()` writes px for a fixed width and keeps the window share for a column span, which is exact only at the design width because the gaps inside the span no longer scale. The pointer-target check measures each value at its own size. The JS readers multiply by the root font size over 16.

## Merge semantics

Atomic CSS resolves conflicts by sheet order, which is not what an author means. Three rules keep it predictable:

- Inside one style object, the last declaration of a property wins: the compiler keeps one declaration per property identity and registers only that atom, so an overridden value never ships.
- Between style objects, only recipes merge. A compiled recipe is a set of layers keyed by property identity; the runtime assigns layers in order and joins the values.
- Class arrays are for additive composition. When two entries that can be present together set the same property, the compiler warns and points at recipes. Ternary branches are exclusive and are not compared with each other.

## The reset

`reset.ts` ships in the `reset` layer, so every atom beats it. Two choices in it need a reason:

- `min-width: 0` on every element. A flex or grid item no longer refuses to shrink below its content, so a long word or a wide child cannot push a row past its container. An item that must keep its content width says so with `minInlineSize: 'auto'`, which works in flex and grid alike. A `<button>` gets `auto` back in the reset: a label squeezed into a grid track (`white-space: nowrap` included) is never what a site means.
- Reduced motion sets every duration to 0.01ms and every animation to one run, with `!important`. A site that wraps its motion in `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference` keeps safe fades; this rule has nothing for an agent to forget, and that is worth more here.

iOS zooms the page into a form field with text under 16px. The reset does not set a size for fields: `font-size` cannot read the field's own preset, so a floor of `max(16px, 1em)` with `!important` shrank a large field to its parent's size. The skill says to give a field a preset of 16px or more on mobile.

The reset removes the tap highlight, and `hover` never applies on a touch screen, so a tap shows nothing unless the element has an `:active` style. The skill says to give every touch target one.

## Hover, focus and overflow

`hover` is `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) &:hover`, so a tap on a touch screen leaves nothing stuck. A `:hover` written in a selector key would skip that, so `normalize` rejects it (`HOVER_NEEDS_CONDITION`), and `buildConditions()` throws on a token condition with `:hover` that does not start with the same media query (`HOVER_MEDIA` and `mentionsHover()` in `compiler/selector.ts`). `outlineStyle: 'none'` or `'hidden'`, or an `outlineWidth` of zero in any unit, is an error (`OUTLINE_REMOVED`): an atom beats the reset's `:focus-visible` ring wherever it applies. `overflow: 'hidden'` warns (`OVERFLOW_HIDDEN`): it makes a scroll container, which stops `position: sticky` inside it, where `clip` only cuts. `clip` makes no block formatting context, so a block box that contained floats or margins with `hidden` adds `display: 'flow-root'`. The failure is silent: a child's negative margin that cropped it makes the box taller. A flex or grid box contains margins on its own. `transitionProperty: 'display'` is not a layout transition: with `allow-discrete` it switches once, at the end (`DISCRETE_PROPS`).

## Escape hatches

The compiler's rules are strict on purpose, so the way out has to be explicit and visible. `unsafe: { ... }` inside a style block emits its properties as written: `normalize` skips the unit, shorthand, typography, and layout rules for them, the report's lint leaves them out, and every one is listed under `report.unsafe` with its file and path. Their atoms carry an `unsafe-` prefix and a separate registry key, so a safe and an unsafe spelling of the same declaration never share a name.

`// visio-ignore CODE: reason` (`compiler/ignore.ts`) silences a warning or a report finding at its location. The extractor reads the file's comments after the evaluator has recorded every key span, attaches each directive to the outermost key that starts on the line it covers, drops the warnings it covers, and hands the rest to the project. `buildReport` drops covered finding locations (a finding with locations left keeps them) and turns a directive that covered nothing into `IGNORE_UNUSED`. The tokens module is read the same way against the object literal passed to `defineTokens()`, so `TOKEN_UNUSED` is ignored next to the token. Errors cannot be ignored: an error rejects a declaration, and `unsafe` is the answer for that. A directive without a reason, or naming an error, is itself an error.

## Lint and the compiler

The compiler keeps every check about what a style means: units, shorthands, runtime values, typography, layout animations, class arrays, and the report. It has the tokens and the stylesheet, so it can say which token a value nearly is. A lint rule would repeat those checks with less information, so none does, `visio-ignore` included.

Conventions about the shape of a file go to `@visio/oxlint-plugin` (`packages/oxlint-plugin/DESIGN.md`), because oxlint shows them in the editor before a build runs. For styling that is two rules: `stylesheet-once` (`@visio/styling/css` only in `src/app.tsx`) and `style-prop-vars` (an element's `style` sets only `cssVars()` names, as `[v.x.name]`).

## Specificity and layers

With natural specificity, `.x:hover` beats `.desktop-x` regardless of order, and `[data-theme=dark] .x` beats both. That makes "later group wins" a lie in exactly the cases that matter. So the emitter wraps every selector part except the atom class itself in `:where()`: `.hover-o-0_5:where(:hover)`, `:where([data-theme=dark]) .dark-c-paper`, `.child-any-mbs-dp8 > :where(*)`. Every atom is (0,1,0) plus any pseudo-element, and the group order in the sheet decides. `&` may sit inside a functional pseudo-class: with `&` at the top level the whole pseudo-class is wrapped (`.x:where(:is(.a .x, .b .x))`); without one, the first pseudo-class that holds `&` carries the class and its arguments are templates in turn (`.parent:has(&)` is `:where(.parent):has(.x)`, `div:has(.a &)` is `:where(div):has(:where(.a) .x)`), so the count stays at one class.

Unlayered CSS always beats layered CSS, whatever the specificity. A project that imports third-party stylesheets and needs atoms to win over them puts the vendor CSS in a layer (`@import url(...) layer(vendor)`). The stylesheets of the visio packages are already in a layer (see "Package stylesheets"). The sheet is always layered and its selectors always uniform; neither is an option.

### Package stylesheets

A visio package that needs CSS declares it in its `package.json`: `"visio": { "stylesheets": ["lenis/dist/lenis.css"] }`. A path resolves from the package that declares it, so it can name a file of a dependency or its own (`./src/x.css`). At startup the plugin follows the site's `visio` and `@visio/*` dependencies, and theirs, and puts each declared stylesheet in the `reset` layer after the reset, a dependency's before its dependent's. A package the site does not install adds nothing. A declared file that does not resolve stops the plugin with the package and the path.

A package never imports a `.css` file: Vite gives each JS chunk its own CSS file, so the rules would land in the CSS of the shared chunk that holds the package, one more render-blocking request on every page. `packages/visio/test/package-css.test.ts` fails on such an import. `build.cssCodeSplit: false` is no fix: it gives one file, but then the server render links no stylesheet.

## Source maps

The evaluator records where every object key was written. Declarations carry that span, the registry keeps the first origin per atom, and the emitter records the origin of every line. The project turns that into a v3 map, hands it to Lightning CSS as the input map, and cleans the composed result. The Vite plugin returns the map from `load()` and enables `css.devSourcemap`, so devtools shows `app.tsx:42` next to each rule. Vite itself emits no CSS maps in production builds (checked with `build.sourcemap: true` on Vite 8.2), but the sheet comes out of Vite's minifier byte for byte, so with `build.sourcemap` on the plugin emits the map as an asset next to the CSS and appends the `sourceMappingURL` comment (`hidden` skips the comment). A chunk that imports other stylesheets gets them concatenated into the same asset, before or after the sheet; the plugin finds the sheet verbatim in the asset (Vite's chunk-order markers removed, as they are before the file is written) and shifts the map's generated positions to where it landed (`asset-map.ts`). If the sheet is not in any CSS asset verbatim, another plugin rewrote it and the map is dropped with a build warning that says so. Every build also writes the shipped sheet and map to `.visio/app.css` and `.visio/app.css.map`.

## Fonts

Fonts are config the build applies; images are content a page places. A font is declared once in the tokens and the CSS applies it through the type presets, so no project code renders one, and font subsetting has no public API. An image sits at one place in the markup, many per page, so it needs `<Image>`, the `?responsive` and `?component` imports, `remoteImage()` for a URL known at runtime, and the image types for props: `@visio/image-optimizer` keeps its own package and public entry. It touches styling only through `sizes()`, which the compiler reads from the `?responsive&sizes=` query, with no import either way. WebGL text (MSDF, not built) needs a glyph atlas, not a WOFF2: a project that needs it reads the font from `t.fonts` and builds the atlas in its own code; the build has no public font API (decided 2026-10-21).

`src/fonts/` is a library in plain Node, with no Vite code: `optimizeFont({ src, subset, cacheDir, axes })` subsets with HarfBuzz, pins the variable axes `axes` names (an axis left out stays variable; with every axis pinned the file is a static instance, the variation tables are dropped, and the advances are those of the instance), re-encodes to WOFF2, and caches by content, subset, axes, and encoder versions, so Bun and Node share the cache. The styling plugin owns the Vite side. `Project.optimizeFonts()` runs it for every token font source with a `subset`, after the scan, because `subset: 'used'` is printable ASCII plus every character the compiled files write in JSX text, strings, and templates. A hot update that adds a character re-subsets and reloads, since the file name is a content hash.

A source can list its subsets, `subset: ['latin', 'latin-ext']`. Each entry is one call to `optimizeFont`, one file, and one `@font-face` rule with the source's family, weight, style and display and the entry's `unicode-range`, as Google Fonts does it. The browser loads a file only when the page draws a character in its range. A `FontFile` records its source (`index`) and its place in the font's files (`face`): the sources in order, and each source's list in order. `fontUrls()`, `fontRanges()` and `tokensToCss` use that order, and so does `t.fonts.x.urls` at runtime, so `url` is the first file of the first source, the one to preload. A single subset is a list of one, so its output does not change. `optimizeFonts()` rejects `used` in a list (it is the only subset), an empty list, and `latin-ext` on a face with no face of the same weight and style that draws ASCII: the preset is Google's exact range, with no ASCII.

Fallback metrics come from the same library. They are measured one time for each weight of a font, on the whole source file of the first upright local source of that weight (an italic only when the font has no upright file: a face measured from an italic would be declared upright), not on each subset. A range (`'300 700'`) gets one face with no `font-weight`: a face declared `300 700` matches text at 700, so the browser would not fake a bold, and regular Arial would stand in for the bold cut. One file per font gave every weight the metrics of one cut, so a heading in another weight rewrapped when the font arrived (#371). `fontMetrics()` reads `head`, `hhea`, `OS/2`, `hmtx`, `cmap` and `name` itself (`tables.ts`; no font parser dependency) from the first font of a TTC, with no outlines. When `OS/2` sets `USE_TYPO_METRICS`, the typographic metrics replace `hhea`'s, as in a browser. The family name is name id 16, else id 1: the Windows US English record first, then a Unicode or Mac English one, then any other; platform 2 (deprecated ISO) and platforms above 3 are skipped. It pins the axes first, so a bold instance gives the bold metrics. `matchFallback()` walks the token's `fallback` list and takes the first family in `FALLBACK_METRICS`, a twelve-row table of the system faces people name (Arial, Helvetica, Helvetica Neue, Segoe UI, Roboto, Verdana, Trebuchet MS, Times New Roman, Georgia, Courier New, Menlo, Monaco; Menlo and Monaco measured with `readFontMetrics` on the macOS 26 files, the other rows from capsize, MIT), each with the full and PostScript names `local()` loads its regular face by, since browsers do not match `local()` on a family name. `FALLBACK_BOLD_METRICS` has the bold face of the ten capsize rows; a source of weight 600 or more is matched to it, and a family without one keeps its regular row. Generic families and `ui-*` keywords are passed over; SF Mono is not in the table because macOS only exposes it through `ui-monospace`. The average width is weighted by capsize's English letter frequencies, so a row copied from capsize and a row measured here agree. `fallbackFace()` is capsize's arithmetic: `size-adjust` scales the fallback until its average character is as wide as the web font's, then ascent, descent, and line gap are the web font's in that scaled em. `tokensToCss` emits each result as an `@font-face` named `<Family> Fallback` with `src: local()` and the source's `font-weight` (`bold` is 700, `normal` 400), listed second in the family stack, so the swap moves nothing. In the client build the plugin emits each file as an asset and hands `tokensToCss` the `__VITE_ASSET__` placeholder for `url()`; in dev a middleware serves the bytes from memory. Every source with a `subset` is subsetted (the cache makes that cheap); only fonts something references are emitted into the bundle and listed in the sheet.

The runtime URL is on the token, not in a virtual module. `defineTokens()` takes a second argument the plugin fills in by transforming the tokens module (its public type has one parameter, so a site cannot write it): `{ fontUrls: { mono: [import.meta.ROLLUP_FILE_URL_x] } }` in the client build (the bundler resolves it), the final asset path in the SSR build, and the dev middleware path in serve. Font names are content hashes and the client build emits them under a fixed file name, so a server build derives the same path whether the client build ran before it, in the same process, or not at all (`vite build --ssr`); the client build checks that the name it wrote matches. The path is the client environment's `build.assetsDir` under `base` (a bare name when the dir is empty), passed through `experimental.renderBuiltUrl` the way Vite passes the client's own asset URLs, so a CDN prefix reaches the server bundle too; a hook that returns a runtime expression cannot be baked and falls back to the base path with a warning. Two token fonts on one file with the same subset and axes get one name and one asset, and every build emits its assets afresh so watch mode and repeated builder runs never reference a previous build's ids. So `t.fonts.mono.url` is a string wherever the tokens module runs, including the prerendered document.

### The subsetter

Its goals: ship only the glyphs the site uses and keep every OpenType feature the kept text can use; pin a variable font to one instance when the design uses one weight; encode each file once, then read it from a cache in Bun and in Node; and fail with a clear error, never an empty font.

```
font.otf ──readFileSync──► source bytes
   │
   ├── unicodeRangeOf(subset) ──► unicode-range (parsed and checked)
   ├── cacheKey ──► <cacheDir>/<key>.woff2 ── a whole WOFF2 file? ──► return it (cached: true)
   │
   └── subsetTtf: HarfBuzz wasm ──► TTF bytes (subset, all layout features, axes pinned)
         └── encodeWoff2: wawoff2, one encode at a time ──► WOFF2 bytes
               └── writeCache: <key>.woff2.<pid>.tmp, then rename ──► return (cached: false)
```

`optimizeFont` returns `{ bytes, name, unicodeRange, cached }`; `name` is `<basename>-<hash8>.woff2`, the hash of the output bytes. `subset` is a preset name, `{ unicodeRange }` or `{ chars }`; the plugin makes `subset: 'used'` into `{ chars }`. `src/fonts/index.ts` exports what the rest of the package uses; the tests import the steps in between from their files.

- **HarfBuzz** (`harfbuzz-subset.ts`) loads `harfbuzz-subset.wasm` from `harfbuzzjs` once per process; a failed load is tried again on the next call. It is a WASI reactor with no imports that grows its own memory. The source bytes are copied into the wasm heap, and the buffer, subset input and face are freed in `finally` blocks, so an error leaks nothing; axis tags are checked before the first allocation. HarfBuzz keeps only a short list of layout features by default, which loses a stylistic set, `case` or small caps the design turns on with `font-feature-settings`, so the subsetter keeps every feature (`hb-subset --layout-features='*'`); a feature whose lookups touch no kept character is still pruned. `hb_subset_or_fail` cannot tell a WOFF file, a broken file and a full heap apart, so its error asks whether the source is an OTF or TTF.
- **Variable axes**: `axes: { wght: 700 }` pins each listed axis with `hb_subset_input_pin_axis_location`. An axis the font lacks is an error. HarfBuzz keeps name ids 0 to 6 only, so a pinned font reports the family name of the default instance.
- **WOFF2** (`woff2.ts`) loads `wawoff2` on the first cache miss, because it parses a 950 kB Emscripten module. `compress` returns a view into the wasm heap that the next call overwrites, so encodes run one at a time in a promise queue and each result is copied out first. Without the queue, fonts encoded together shipped each other's bytes.
- **Cache** (`cache.ts`): one file per result, `<cacheDir>/<key>.woff2`, the key a sha256 of `CACHE_VERSION` (raise it when an older version could write a bad entry; version 2 dropped the entries the concurrent encode wrote), the source bytes, the unicode-range, the sorted pinned axes, `SUBSET_SETTINGS`, and the versions of `harfbuzzjs` and `wawoff2`. `versionOf` walks up from the package's main entry to its `package.json`, because `harfbuzzjs/package.json` is not exported; the walk works on Windows paths too. A read checks the `wOF2` signature and the header length, and encodes again on a mismatch. A write goes to `<key>.woff2.<pid>.tmp` and is renamed, so a killed build never leaves half a file under the key. The plugin puts the cache in `visio-fonts` under the Vite cache directory.
- **Presets**: `PRESET_RANGES` holds Google Fonts' `latin`, `latin-ext`, `cyrillic`, `cyrillic-ext`, `greek`, `greek-ext` and `vietnamese`, each the `unicode-range` `fonts.googleapis.com` sends (a test compares them); `vietnamese` includes its combining marks. Google sends each subset as its own file, so the ranges do not overlap and `latin-ext` has no ASCII.
- **Errors** start with `[@visio/styling]`, and `optimizeFont` adds the source path and keeps the original as `cause`: an unknown preset; a unicode-range that is empty, does not parse, or holds a reversed range or one above U+10FFFF; an empty `chars`; an axis tag that is not four characters or that the font lacks; a wasm heap with no room for the font or the subset input; a font HarfBuzz cannot subset; a wasm with no subsetter; and a font with no `head`, `hhea` or `hmtx` table.

## Light and dark

`theme()`, `setTheme()`, `toggleTheme()`, `restoreTheme()` and `THEME_SCRIPT` keep the page's light or dark mode: `[data-theme=dark]` on `<html>`, the attribute the `dark` theme of the tokens keys on. The inline script and the signal read the same storage key (`visio-theme`), and only a toggle saves it, so a visitor who never chose follows the system preference on every load. The server renders `light`, so `restoreTheme()` runs after hydration; the attribute is already right from the script, and only the signal changes. One module owns the key and the attribute, so the script and the signal cannot disagree. It is the one part of the package with a Solid runtime, so `solid-js` is a peer.

**Route themes.** `routeThemes(t)` (`route-themes.ts`) is a router extension: a page names `theme` in its meta, `light` or a theme of the tokens, and wins over the visitor's mode. The router does not know the tokens, so the theme names (for the type of `meta.theme`, through `Register`) and the page colours come with the call. It works on the router's seams, so the router gains no styling code:

- `head` puts `<meta name="theme-color">` and, on a themed page, a one-line script that sets `<html data-theme>` into the head. `<html>` itself is sent before a streamed page's data, so the server cannot write the theme on it; the head waits for the meta, so the script runs before the body paints. Both are `always` tags: they describe how the page looks, so a `noindex` page keeps them.
- `theme-color` is a literal colour, never a variable, so it is the value of `colors.page` in that theme, and in the base palette on a page without a theme (with a light and a dark tag when the tokens have `dark`). `colors.page` is explicit, not read from the body's style: the call throws `PAGE_COLOR_MISSING` without it.
- `root` writes `<html data-theme>` on every page after: the page's theme, or `theme()` once `restoreTheme()` has read it. With the extension on, `show()` in `theme.ts` leaves `<html>` alone, so one writer owns it; the visitor's choice is still saved for the next page without a theme.
- `state` calls `meta()` again. A throw there means no theme: the head reports it, and an error in a state memo would halt the app.

`tokensToCss` writes every theme with each colour any theme sets, the missing ones from the base, and a `[data-theme=light]` block with the base values. A theme inside another then shows its own palette: the leaving page of a transition keeps its theme while `<html>` already has the next one (`@visio/transitions` pins it), and a `dark` block inside a `sand` page does not show sand's colours that dark leaves out.

## Pruning

A token variable ships only if something references it: a `var()` in a compiled declaration, or a member expression like `t.colors.accent` anywhere in a compiled file, including plain JS. Reading a whole group (`t.colors`, or `const { colors } = t`) keeps the group; reading `t.source`, or the tokens object without a member (`Object.keys(t)`, `t` passed to a function), keeps every token. A parameter or local with the same name as the import hides it, so its reads do not count. The core fluid variables always ship. Pruned names appear in the report so nothing disappears silently. A colour leaf also has `alpha(amount)`, which gives `color-mix(in srgb, var(--colors-x) n%, transparent)`. The compiler evaluates `t.colors.x.alpha(n)` with a literal amount (`ALPHA_NEEDS_AMOUNT`, `ALPHA_NEEDS_COLOR`), and the member read keeps the token. Mixing the variable, not its value, keeps the colour on the theme; a helper of the site's own that returns the same string is a call the compiler cannot read (`CALL_NOT_STATIC`).

## Options

`styling()` takes no options, because an agent that can turn a rule off will do it to make an error go away. The tokens module is always `src/styles/tokens.ts` (`TOKENS_PATH` in `project.ts`). The CSS output targets the oldest browsers that know cascade layers (`['defaults and fully supports css-cascade-layers']`), because the sheet is built on layers. Findings always fail the build, a type preset always owns the font metrics, the compiler reads every `src/**/*.{ts,tsx}`, the reset always ships (with the defaults of `<Image>` from `@visio/image-optimizer`: the `<picture>` fills its box, the `<img>` fills the `<picture>`), and unused tokens are always pruned. `vite.ts` calls the plugin with no switches. `plugin.ts` holds the plugin with the switches that only tests use (`tokens`, `writeArtifacts`, `strictReport`, `typography: 'open'`, `prune: false`); it is not a package entry.

`visio-styling check` has no options either. It reads `src/styles/tokens.ts` and fails like the build. `--root` is left in for the tests and is not in the help.

The screens are four fixed names, `mobile`, `tablet`, `desktop` and `widescreen`, so every project has the same keys in its per-screen values and the same conditions, and an agent never guesses between `tablet`, `tab` and `ipad`. A screen's start is its own `from`, desktop's too: a separate `breakpoints.dt` was the same number in a second place, and `dt` a second name for desktop.

## Dependencies

The fonts take two: `harfbuzzjs` (HarfBuzz as wasm) and `wawoff2` (Google's WOFF2 encoder as wasm).

`subset: 'used'` decodes JSX text with `html-entities`, by the HTML5 rules. Solid's compiler leaves an entity in a template for the browser to decode, and decodes one in a component's children itself, and a test holds `html-entities` to the compiler.

## Constraints on the plugin source

The CLI shim runs on Node and loads this package from source through Node's type stripping. No enums, no namespaces, no parameter properties, no decorators. `import type` everywhere types are used.

## Not yet built

- `TARGET_TOO_SMALL` reads a parent's box only from a single scaled `grid-auto-rows` or a scaled flex-row height; `grid-template-rows`, `1fr` tracks, column directions, and parents in another component fall back to the child's own padding estimate.
- Removal of the `.tmp` files a killed build leaves in the font cache.
- `subset: 'used'` reads source text and the case transforms styles apply. Text built at runtime from locale formatting or a CMS is not covered; use a preset for that.
